questions.stem: In all forms of chromatography, what separates the components of a mixture?
options: Differences in how strongly components interact with the stationary and mobile phases
Differences in the masses of the components, so heavier components always move slowest
Differences in colour, so only coloured components can be separated from each other
Differences in the charges of components, so neutral molecules cannot be separated at all
questions.explanation: Each component distributes itself between the stationary and mobile phases according to the strength of its interactions, so components move at different rates. Colourless and neutral substances can be separated too.

questions.stem: In thin layer chromatography (TLC), what are the stationary and mobile phases?
options: A column packed with resin beads; a gas pumped at high pressure
A glass plate with no coating; the mixture being analysed
A thin coating of silica or alumina on a plate; a liquid solvent
A liquid solvent soaked into paper; an inert carrier gas
questions.explanation: In TLC the stationary phase is a thin layer of an adsorbent such as silica gel on a glass, plastic or aluminium plate, and the mobile phase is a solvent that rises up the plate.

questions.stem: In gas chromatography (GC), what is the mobile phase?
options: An unreactive carrier gas, such as helium or nitrogen
A polar liquid solvent pumped through at high pressure
A solid adsorbent, such as silica, coating the column
The vaporised sample itself, without any other gas
questions.explanation: In GC an inert carrier gas carries the vaporised sample through a column whose inner surface is coated with a liquid or solid stationary phase. A liquid mobile phase under pressure describes HPLC.

questions.stem: Why is high pressure used to push the mobile phase through an HPLC column?
options: The pressure decomposes the sample into its elements for detection
The column is packed with very small particles that resist the flow of liquid
The pressure vaporises the sample so that it can be carried as a gas
The pressure increases the charge on ions so they bind to the resin
questions.explanation: Very fine stationary-phase particles give a large surface area and good separation, but liquid will only flow through them quickly under high pressure. The sample stays in solution and is not vaporised or decomposed.

questions.stem: A TLC plate has a polar silica stationary phase and a non-polar solvent. Which component of a mixture will travel furthest?
options: The component with the most O-H groups
The component that is an ionic salt
The least polar component
The most polar component
questions.explanation: Polar components are attracted strongly to the polar silica and spend more time adsorbed, so they move slowly. The least polar component spends more time dissolved in the non-polar solvent and travels furthest.

questions.stem: Propan-1-ol, propanoic acid and hexane are separated by TLC on polar silica with a non-polar solvent. What is the order of RF values, from highest to lowest?
options: Propan-1-ol, then hexane, then propanoic acid
Hexane, then propanoic acid, then propan-1-ol
Hexane, then propan-1-ol, then propanoic acid
Propanoic acid, then propan-1-ol, then hexane
questions.explanation: Hexane is non-polar, so it is least attracted to silica and moves furthest. Propanoic acid, with its carboxyl group able to form more hydrogen bonds, interacts most strongly with silica and has the lowest RF.

questions.stem: In a reversed-phase HPLC column, the stationary phase is non-polar and the mobile phase is a polar water-methanol mixture. Which compound has the shortest retention time?
options: Glucose, which has many O-H groups
Octane, which is a non-polar alkane
Hexan-1-ol, which has one O-H group
Hexanoic acid, with a long chain
questions.explanation: With a non-polar stationary phase, the most polar compound interacts least with it and most with the polar mobile phase, so it leaves the column first. Octane is retained longest.

questions.stem: In gas chromatography, compound P has a shorter retention time than compound Q under the same conditions. What can be concluded?
options: P interacts less strongly with the stationary phase than Q does
P is present in a larger amount in the sample than Q is
P has a larger molar mass and higher boiling point than Q
P interacts more strongly with the stationary phase than Q
questions.explanation: Retention time is the time from injection to detection; a component that interacts weakly with the stationary phase spends more time in the carrier gas and elutes first. The amount present affects peak area, not retention time.

questions.stem: How is the RF value of a spot on a TLC plate calculated?
options: Distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent front, both from the baseline
Distance moved by the solvent front ÷ distance moved by the spot, both from the baseline
Distance moved by the spot ÷ the total length of the plate from bottom to top
Distance moved by the spot − distance moved by the solvent front, from the baseline
questions.explanation: RF is the ratio of the distance moved by the component to the distance moved by the solvent front, measured from the baseline. It is always between 0 and 1.

questions.stem: On a TLC plate, a spot moves 2.7 cm from the baseline and the solvent front moves 7.5 cm. What is the RF value?
questions.explanation: RF = 2.7 ÷ 7.5 = 0.36. Inverting the ratio gives 2.8, which is impossible because an RF value cannot exceed 1.

questions.stem: A dye has an RF of 0.42 in a given solvent. On a plate where the solvent front moves 6.5 cm from the baseline, how far does the dye travel?
options: 15 cm
6.1 cm
2.7 cm
questions.explanation: Distance moved = RF × distance of solvent front = 0.42 × 6.5 = 2.7 cm. Dividing 6.5 by 0.42 gives a distance longer than the solvent front, which is impossible.

questions.stem: A suspected banned stimulant in an athlete's urine gives a GC peak at 6.42 min. Which further evidence most strengthens identification of the compound?
options: A pure standard of the stimulant gives a peak at 6.42 min on the same column and conditions
The peak at 6.42 min is the largest peak on the chromatogram of the urine sample
A standard of the stimulant gives a peak at 6.42 min on a different column at a higher temperature
The urine sample gives exactly one peak, at 6.42 min, when the column temperature is changed
questions.explanation: Retention time depends on the column, temperature and flow rate, so a match is meaningful only when the standard is run under identical conditions. Peak size reflects the amount present, not identity.

questions.stem: A TLC of a newly synthesised drug shows one large spot and one faint spot with a different RF. What does this indicate?
options: The solvent front was measured from the wrong line
The sample contains a small amount of an impurity
The drug has decomposed completely into one product
The drug is pure, since the main spot is the largest
questions.explanation: A pure substance gives a single spot; a second spot with a different RF shows another component, here a minor impurity. A single compound does not give two spots under the same conditions.

questions.stem: Why is the baseline on a TLC plate drawn in pencil and placed above the level of the solvent in the tank?
options: Pencil reacts with the stationary phase, and the solvent must cover the baseline
Pencil makes the spots more polar, and the solvent must evaporate before it rises
Pencil does not dissolve and move, and the spots must not dissolve into the solvent pool
Pencil absorbs the solvent faster, and the spots must dissolve into the solvent pool
questions.explanation: Graphite is insoluble in the solvent, whereas ink would itself separate. If the baseline were below the solvent surface, the samples would wash off into the solvent instead of travelling up the plate.

questions.stem: Two chromatograms of an orange juice sample are compared. On TLC, two components have the same RF. Which conclusion is justified?
options: They must be the same compound, because two compounds can never have the same RF in one solvent
They must be different compounds, because each compound in a mixture has a different RF value
They cannot be compared, because RF values are only meaningful for coloured compounds on paper
They may be the same compound, but the result should be confirmed in another solvent or technique
questions.explanation: Different compounds can coincidentally have the same RF in one solvent, so a matching RF suggests but does not prove identity. Repeating with another solvent or technique strengthens the conclusion.

questions.stem: A cation exchange resin carries Na⁺ ions. Water containing Ca²⁺ ions passes through it. Which equation represents the exchange?
options: 2R⁻Na⁺(s) + Ca²⁺(aq) ⇌ (R⁻)₂Ca²⁺(s) + Na₂(g)
R⁺Na⁻(s) + Ca²⁺(aq) ⇌ R⁺Ca²⁺(s) + Na⁻(aq)
2R⁻Na⁺(s) + Ca²⁺(aq) ⇌ (R⁻)₂Ca²⁺(s) + 2Na⁺(aq)
R⁻Na⁺(s) + Ca²⁺(aq) ⇌ R⁻Ca²⁺(s) + Na⁺(aq)
questions.explanation: Each Ca²⁺ ion takes the place of two Na⁺ ions on the negatively charged resin, keeping charges balanced. The one-for-one equation leaves the charges unbalanced.

questions.stem: A cation exchange resin used to remove Ca²⁺ from water becomes saturated. Using equilibrium principles, why does flushing it with concentrated sodium chloride solution regenerate it?
options: The salt raises the temperature of the resin, which always favours release of Ca²⁺ ions
The Na⁺ ions react with Ca²⁺ to form a precipitate that is rinsed off the resin
The high [Na⁺] shifts the exchange equilibrium so Ca²⁺ is released and Na⁺ binds again
The chloride ions bind to the negative sites, pushing Ca²⁺ off as calcium chloride crystals
questions.explanation: For 2R⁻Na⁺ + Ca²⁺ ⇌ (R⁻)₂Ca²⁺ + 2Na⁺, a large excess of Na⁺ shifts the equilibrium to the left by Le Châtelier's principle, replacing Ca²⁺ on the resin with Na⁺. Chloride ions are not attracted to the negative resin sites.

questions.stem: In ion chromatography with a cation exchange column, which ion is usually held most strongly by the resin?
options: Al³⁺, because it has the highest charge
Na⁺, because it has the lowest charge
Cl⁻, because it is an anion
K⁺, because it is a larger ion
questions.explanation: Cations with higher charges are attracted more strongly to the negative sites of the resin, so they are retained longer. Anions are not held by a cation exchange resin at all.

questions.stem: What is the electron configuration of a calcium atom in subshell notation?
options: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d²
1s² 2s⁸ 2p⁸ 3s² 3p²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁸
questions.explanation: Calcium has 20 electrons; after 3p⁶ the next subshell to fill is 4s, which is lower in energy than 3d. A p subshell holds at most six electrons, so 3p⁸ is impossible.

questions.stem: What is the electron configuration of the Fe²⁺ ion (iron has atomic number 26)?
options: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁴ 4s²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁸
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ 4s²
questions.explanation: Fe²⁺ has 24 electrons. When a transition metal atom forms a cation, the 4s electrons are lost before the 3d electrons, leaving 3d⁶. The configuration with 4s² is the neutral atom.

questions.stem: What is the electron configuration of the sulfide ion, S²⁻ (sulfur has atomic number 16)?
options: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p²
questions.explanation: S²⁻ has 18 electrons, gaining two to fill the 3p subshell. 3p⁴ is the neutral sulfur atom, and 4s² would add two electrons too many.

questions.stem: Strontium has atomic number 38. Which is its electron configuration?
options: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p⁶ 5s²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p⁸
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 4p⁶ 5s² 4d¹⁰
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁶ 4d²
questions.explanation: After 4p⁶ (36 electrons, krypton), the remaining two electrons enter 5s, which fills before 4d. A p subshell cannot hold eight electrons, 3d fills before 4p, and 4d fills only after 5s.

questions.stem: What happens to an electron in an atom when the atom absorbs a photon of exactly the right energy?
options: It moves from a lower energy level to a higher energy level
It moves from a higher energy level to a lower energy level
It leaves the nucleus and becomes a proton in the atom
It stays in its energy level but starts to move faster
questions.explanation: Absorbed energy promotes the electron to a higher energy level, producing an excited state. Moving to a lower level releases energy as emitted light.

questions.stem: In a flame test, why does a heated sodium compound emit yellow-orange light?
options: The sodium compound burns in oxygen, and the heat released glows yellow-orange
Sodium atoms lose protons in the flame, releasing energy as visible light
Excited electrons fall to lower energy levels, emitting photons of specific energies
Electrons absorb the yellow-orange light of the flame and remove it from the spectrum
questions.explanation: The flame excites electrons to higher levels; as they return to lower levels they emit photons whose energies equal the energy gaps, giving sodium's characteristic colour. No protons are lost, and the colour is not just glowing heat.

questions.stem: A compound gives a blue-green colour in a flame test. Which metal is most likely present?
options: Potassium
Lithium
Copper
Sodium
questions.explanation: Copper compounds give a blue-green flame. Sodium gives yellow-orange, potassium lilac and lithium red.

questions.stem: Why are the wavelengths emitted and absorbed by an element unique to that element?
options: Each element has its own nuclear charge, so its energy level differences are unique
Each element has its own number of neutrons, so its isotopes absorb different light
Each element is a different colour as a solid, which fixes the light it can emit
Each element burns at its own temperature, which fixes the wavelengths of its flame
questions.explanation: Energy levels depend on the nuclear charge and electron arrangement, which differ for every element, so the energy gaps, and hence the wavelengths, are unique. Isotopes of one element have essentially the same spectrum.

questions.stem: A flame test gives an orange-yellow flame that hides any other colour. Why is AAS more useful than a flame test for detecting potassium in this sample?
options: AAS measures absorption at a wavelength specific to potassium, so sodium does not interfere
AAS heats the sample to a lower temperature, so the sodium no longer emits any light at all
AAS uses a lamp of every element at once, so all of the colours can be seen together
AAS removes the sodium from the sample by ion exchange before the potassium is measured
questions.explanation: AAS uses light of a wavelength characteristic of the element being measured and detects only the absorption at that wavelength, so a strong sodium emission does not mask potassium. It uses a lamp made of the target element, not of every element.

questions.stem: In atomic absorption spectroscopy, why is the hollow cathode lamp made of the element being measured?
options: It emits every visible wavelength, so any element in the sample can absorb
It emits exactly the wavelengths that atoms of that element absorb
It reacts with the sample to form a coloured compound that is measured
It heats the sample enough to break it into separate atoms in the flame
questions.explanation: Excited atoms in the lamp emit the element's characteristic wavelengths, which are the same wavelengths that ground-state atoms of the element in the flame absorb. The flame, not the lamp, atomises the sample.

questions.stem: What is the role of the flame (or furnace) in an atomic absorption spectrometer?
options: To burn off the element being measured so that only impurities remain
To convert the sample into free atoms that can absorb the lamp's light
To excite all the atoms so they emit light that is measured by the detector
To select a single wavelength from the light emitted by the lamp
questions.explanation: The flame atomises the sample so that free ground-state atoms are present to absorb the radiation. Selecting a single wavelength is the job of the monochromator.

questions.stem: In AAS, what does the monochromator do?
options: Converts the sample solution into a fine spray of droplets
Supplies the electric current that makes the lamp glow
Measures the temperature of the flame during the analysis
Selects one characteristic wavelength to pass to the detector
questions.explanation: The monochromator isolates one wavelength that the element absorbs and passes it to the detector, which measures its intensity. The nebuliser, not the monochromator, sprays the sample.

questions.stem: In AAS, how is the concentration of an element related to the measurement made?
options: A higher concentration gives a longer wavelength of light at the detector
A higher concentration gives a brighter flame colour seen by the detector
A higher concentration gives a higher absorbance, as more light is absorbed
A higher concentration gives a lower absorbance, as less light is absorbed
questions.explanation: More atoms in the flame absorb more of the lamp's radiation, so absorbance increases with concentration, approximately in proportion over the working range. The wavelength is fixed by the element.

questions.stem: AAS zinc standards of 0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0 and 4.0 mg L⁻¹ give absorbances of 0, 0.085, 0.170, 0.255 and 0.340. A water sample diluted 1 in 20 gives 0.204. What is the zinc concentration of the undiluted water?
options: 0.12 mg L⁻¹
4.1 mg L⁻¹
48 mg L⁻¹
2.4 mg L⁻¹
questions.explanation: The calibration slope is 0.085 per mg L⁻¹, so the diluted sample is 0.204 ÷ 0.085 = 2.4 mg L⁻¹. The undiluted water is 20 times this, 48 mg L⁻¹. Forgetting the dilution gives 2.4 mg L⁻¹.

questions.stem: A sample's absorbance in AAS is higher than that of the most concentrated standard. What should the analyst do?
options: Report the concentration of the highest standard as the sample concentration
Increase the flame temperature until the absorbance drops into the range
Dilute the sample by a known factor so its absorbance falls within the standards
Extend the calibration line beyond the standards and read the concentration off
questions.explanation: Extrapolation is unreliable because the calibration may not stay linear at high concentrations. Diluting by a known factor brings the reading within the calibrated range, and the factor is used to calculate the original concentration.

questions.stem: Atomic absorption spectroscopy was developed in the 1950s by which scientist?
options: Sir Alan Walsh
Fritz Haber
Linus Pauling
Dmitri Mendeleev
questions.explanation: Sir Alan Walsh developed atomic absorption spectroscopy while working at the CSIRO. Pauling is known for work on chemical bonding, Haber for ammonia synthesis and Mendeleev for the periodic table.

questions.stem: A student plots an AAS calibration graph, but the point for one standard lies well above the line through the other four. What is the best response?
options: Discard all five standards, since one anomaly means none of them are reliable
Use only that point to calculate the sample, since it has the highest absorbance
Remake and re-measure that standard, since it was probably prepared incorrectly
Draw the line through that point, since every measured point must lie on the line
questions.explanation: An outlying standard most likely reflects an error in its preparation or measurement; it should be checked and repeated rather than forcing the line through it. One anomaly does not invalidate the other standards.
